HSBC’s RedCoin stablecoin goes live in Hong Kong: what the launch answers, and what it still doesn’t
summary: HSBC has started rolling out RedCoin, its Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin, to more than 3.3 million users of its PayMe payments app, according to the South China Morning Post. The phased launch began on Friday, 23 October, starting with transfers between users and payments to merchants. Three weeks ago, investingLive flagged that RedCoin had a name but no launch date . That question now has an answer. Two others do not: which blockchain RedCoin runs on, and whether it can ever leave HSBC’s own apps. What happened According to the SCMP, PayMe users can activate a RedCoin wallet with no minimum balance and no extra account-opening steps. Once they update the app, they can select the wallet and send money instantly, through an interface similar to the existing PayMe experience. Full availability is expected before the weekend. Lawrence Li, head of PayMe, told the paper the first phase is about keeping the service stable, avoiding extra hassle for customers and earning their trust. That is a deliberately cautious start for a bank-issued token. The SCMP also reported that HSBC plans to add RedCoin to its Hong Kong mobile banking app by year-end. That would allow instant subscriptions to tokenised money market funds from HK$100, with tokenised gold and third-party funds to follow. HSBC is one of only two firms licensed to issue stablecoins in Hong Kong. title: Heads up: UK retail sales to test the case for further BOE rate hikes
summary: The UK retail sales release will be one of the main items to watch out for in the economic calendar today, especially after the latest inflation and labour market figures have given the BOE plenty to think about ahead of its November meeting. For the September report, retail sales are expected to fall by 0.1% on the month, following a 0.5% increase in August. Meanwhile, retail sales are expected to rise by 1.0% annually - a slowdown from 2.4% previously. The numbers might not be all too interesting on the surface, but they will matter to the broader context in shaping the BOE outlook. UK headline annual inflation climbed to 3.5% in September, with core annual inflation also picking up to 2.8%. That is hardly reassuring for the BOE, especially with policymakers already having to contend with elevated energy prices and the risk of more persistent price pressures. Meanwhile, the labour market gave us a bit of a surprise earlier this week. The unemployment rate surprisingly fell to 4.7%, while real wage growth nudged slightly higher to 3.7%. The numbers might be affected by data quality issues with the ONS but they reflect a modest bounce in labour market conditions regardless. Having said that, the details are less rosy with job vacancies continuing to decline, suggesting that hiring demand is losing momentum. And in any case, one report doesn't make a trend. The UK labour market has been showing signs of softness this year and I would be remiss if I didn't point out that fact.

summary: France October flash services PMI 48.4 vs 50.7 expected Prior 51.2 France October flash manufacturing PMI 49.3 vs 50.5 expected Prior 50.6 France October flash composite PMI 48.4 vs 50.5 expected Prior 51.1 That's not a good sign as the French private sector falls back into contraction in October, amid political and financial concerns. Weighing on activity levels was the sharpest decline in demand for French goods and services since May, which surveyed businesses attributed to heightened uncertainty and economic pressures. The only good news perhaps for the ECB is that the survey's price gauges decreased from September to signal an easing of input cost and output charge inflation rates. Looking at the breakdown, manufacturers and service providers reported steeper declines in demand amid reports of projects being postponed as customers held back on decision making. Meanwhile, French businesses turned pessimistic towards one-year outlook with the future composite index falling to its lowest level since April 2020. That indicates negative corporate sentiment for the first time in close to two years. The more downbeat expectations were often linked to next year's election period, with some companies also expressing concerns regarding public finances. title: What are the main events for today?
summary: EUROPEAN SESSION In the European session, we get the Flash PMIs for the major Eurozone economies and the UK. Given the current growth concerns, disappointing PMIs could add to fears that the recent tightening in financial conditions and the elevated energy prices are starting to strangle the economy. This scenario should result in a dovish repricing further out the curve, with traders pricing in 71 bps of tightening for the ECB by the end of 2027 and 112 bps for the BoE. Better than expected data could quell growth concerns and trigger some relief rallies, but it wouldn't change the bigger picture as central banks will have to remain hawkish due to inflationary pressures stemming from the Middle East conflicts. AMERICAN SESSION In the American session, the main highlight will be the releases of the US Flash PMIs, as the Canadian Retail Sales and the final UMich consumer sentiment won't change anything for the market. Everything said about the Eurozone and UK PMIs is valid for the US PMIs too. The market has shifted its focus from inflation to growth as the conflicts in the Middle East, elevated energy prices, tigthening financial conditions, hawkish Fed and lower fiscal impulse on a Dems victory at the midterm elections are all bearish drivers. Good PMIs could lead to a relief rally on easing growth concerns, but again, they won't change the bigger picture as those negative drivers will remain unchanged. This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.
